screens.title: Understanding UObject and Garbage Collection
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn why Unreal Engine uses a special object model built on top of C++ and how that model changes the way you create and hold references to objects. We start with the core claim: most engine-managed types must derive from the UObject base class. That one decision enables reflection, serialization, networking, editor integration, and a custom garbage collector that walks object references to reclaim memory safely. A concrete example you will practice later is creating a UMyDataContainer class derived from UObject, exposing an integer with UPROPERTY, and instantiating it with NewObject inside an actor. This pattern shows the full chain: UCLASS and UPROPERTY inform the reflection system, the Unreal Header Tool generates glue code, and NewObject registers the instance so the GC can track it. Why this matters in practice: if you use plain C++ new or keep a raw UObject* without UPROPERTY, the engine's GC cannot see the reference and the object can be collected unexpectedly, leading to crashes. A common misconception is to treat UObject pointers like regular pointers; they require the engine's metadata so lifetime is managed correctly. As you explore the screens ahead, watch for the rules around UPROPERTY, Outer objects, NewObject calls, and root objects. By the end you'll understand the safe creation pattern and how to avoid dangling pointers. Consider: what part of your current code would change if its objects needed reflection and GC tracking?

Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Understanding UObject & GC
Understanding UObject and Garbage Collection
Learn the engine's object model, how reflection metadata is produced, and the correct patterns for creating and owning UObjects so they integrate with Unreal's garbage collector.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Concept Map
UObject
→
Reflection
Which feeds editor UI, serialization, and GC.
In this lesson
UObject Basics
Why most engine types inherit from UObject.
Reflection & Macros
UCLASS, UPROPERTY, UFUNCTION and UHT flow.
GC & NewObject
Correct creation and lifetime rules.
Key Takeaway

When a type must be engine-managed, derive from UObject, tag members with UPROPERTY, and create instances with NewObject to ensure reflection and GC integration.

Quick Example
// Create owned UObject inside an actor
MyDataInstance = NewObject<UMyDataContainer>(this);
if (MyDataInstance)
{
  MyDataInstance->MyIntValue = 42;
  MyDataInstance->PrintMyData();
}

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives frame the skills you're about to practice. First, you'll explain the role of the UObject base class: not just a parent type but the foundation for reflection, GC, and editor integration. Understanding this clarifies why many engine systems expect UObject-derived types. Second, you will describe the reflection system and the meaning of UCLASS, UPROPERTY, and UFUNCTION. These macros produce metadata that the Unreal Header Tool parses and transforms into generated code, allowing runtime inspection, Blueprint exposure, and GC tracking. Third, you will understand Unreal's garbage collection for UObjects: how roots, reachability, and the GC pass determine which objects live or are reclaimed. You'll learn the rules that make objects collectible or safe. Fourth, you will identify common pitfalls like creating UObjects with new, missing UPROPERTY on member pointers, or mixing raw C++ smart pointers with engine GC. Each objective includes a concrete practice: create a UObject-derived class, add a UPROPERTY field, instantiate it with NewObject, and observe GC-safe behavior. A common misconception is assuming standard C++ memory rules apply unchanged; we'll contrast them with engine-managed lifetimes so you can avoid crashes and leaks. These objectives guide the hands-on steps later in the chapter.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical skills
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond explanation, this second set of objectives targets practical application. You will correctly use UPROPERTY on UObject member pointers so the garbage collector sees them. That practice includes declaring UPROPERTY for components or nested objects that your class owns. Next, you will instantiate UObjects with NewObject and pass a proper Outer so the created object joins the engine's object hierarchy. A concrete example: inside an actor's BeginPlay you will call NewObject<UMyDataContainer>(this), assign properties, and call a print function to verify the instance behaves as a managed UObject. You will also learn to detect and fix common pitfalls such as using new for UObjects or keeping non-UPROPERTY raw pointers to UObjects. A frequent misconception is to rely on standard smart pointers for UObjects; TSharedPtr and std::unique_ptr are for raw C++ types and do not register pointers with the UObject GC. Finally, you'll work with TWeakObjectPtr when you need non-owning references that must not prevent GC. Each skill is paired with a simple test: create, expose, instantiate, and validate behavior in the editor and during Play. This approach builds confidence and prevents lifetime-related bugs in your projects.

screens.title: What is UObject?
screens.narratorSegment: Start by grounding the definition: UObject is the engine's base class for objects that must be visible to the runtime systems. When a class derives from UObject it gains reflection metadata, serialization hooks, network replication support, editor integration, and eligibility for Unreal's garbage collection. Think of UObject as a contract with the engine: it promises the engine can inspect and manage instances. A concrete example is UActorComponent or UDataAsset; both derive from UObject and therefore appear in the editor and can be saved, replicated, and collected. One common misconception is that UObject is merely a naming convention or a thin wrapper over C++ objects. In reality, UObject participates in engine life-cycle events and requires special creation and ownership patterns. To make this practical, imagine you need a lightweight data holder that the editor can edit and Blueprints can call. You derive from UObject, annotate members with UPROPERTY to expose fields, and annotate functions with UFUNCTION for Blueprint calls. Then you create instances using NewObject so the engine registers them. Without deriving from UObject you lose those runtime features. Key takeaway: whenever a type must be inspected by the engine or be tracked by the GC, it should derive from UObject. Reflect on your recent classes: which need reflection or GC tracking and should therefore be refactored to inherit from UObject?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: UObject is the engine-managed base class that enables reflection, serialization, networking, editor integration, and garbage collection for C++ types.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is UObject?
The engine's foundational, engine-managed class that gives C++ types runtime capabilities.
•
Reflection and editor visibility
UObject types can expose properties and functions to the editor and Blueprints when annotated with macros.
•
Serialization and networking
The engine saves and replicates UObject state using generated metadata and serialization hooks.
•
Garbage collection participation
UObjects are tracked by the engine's garbage collector when references are visible via UPROPERTY or other tracked containers.
Analogy
Think of UObject as a managed file in a system. When it follows the system's rules, tools can inspect, save, and clean it up automatically. Bypass the rules and you lose those services.
Concrete Example
UActorComponent derives from UObject so it appears in the editor, can be saved with the actor, and is tracked by GC. You can add properties to it with UPROPERTY and expose functions to Blueprints with UFUNCTION.
Common Misconception
UObject is not optional for engine-managed features. Treating UObject-like C++ classes as plain objects misses reflection and GC integration and often leads to hidden bugs.
Key Takeaway

Derive from UObject for engine-managed behaviors; it is the entry point for reflection, saving, networking, and GC.

Check Your Understanding

List one feature you would lose if a class did not derive from UObject. How would that affect editor workflows?

screens.title: Reflection System and Macros
screens.narratorSegment: Now let's examine the reflection system and the role of the macros. The reflection system is how Unreal learns about your classes, properties, and functions at runtime. When you add UCLASS, UPROPERTY, or UFUNCTION to your header, the Unreal Header Tool parses those markers and generates additional C++ code — the generated header files — which register type information and property metadata with the engine. A concrete example: declaring UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere) float MyValue declares the property and attaches editor metadata so it appears in Details panels. Importantly, UPROPERTY also signals to the garbage collector that a pointer member should be treated as a live reference. A common misconception is that UPROPERTY only affects editor exposure; in truth it also influences GC behavior and serialization. Practically, this means you should annotate any UObject* members you expect the GC to consider. UFUNCTION controls whether functions are callable from Blueprints or network-replicable depending on flags. The reflection glue enables dynamic creation by name, property iteration, and serialization. If you remove the macros, the engine cannot generate the required metadata and those runtime features break. As you code, treat the macros as both administrative and functional: they change how the engine treats your types, not just how the editor displays them. Reflect on a recent property: would the engine need to see it? If yes, annotate it with UPROPERTY and choose the correct metadata flags.

keyIdea.title: Reflection role
keyIdea.text: UCLASS, UPROPERTY, and UFUNCTION feed UHT which generates runtime metadata enabling editor exposure, serialization, Blueprint access, and GC tracking.

content.html:
Definition
Reflection System and Macros
How macros create metadata consumed by the engine tooling and runtime.
UCLASS marks a class for reflection and enables generation of type registration code.
UPROPERTY adds metadata to fields and ensures the GC and serializer see the member.
UFUNCTION marks functions for Blueprint or network usage and includes runtime metadata.
Architecture — How UHT fits
UHT parses headers with macros and emits generated code. That generated code registers classes, properties, and functions so the runtime knows type layouts, names, and metadata.
Concrete example
UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere) float MyValue; makes MyValue editable, serializable, and visible to the GC as a tracked field. Without UPROPERTY the engine treats the member as an opaque C++ field.
Misconception check
UPROPERTY is more than inspector sugar; it is essential for correct GC tracking and serialization of UObjects and their members.
Key Takeaway

Use the macros intentionally: they produce metadata that the engine relies on for runtime features and GC safety.

Try this

Annotate a property with UPROPERTY and confirm it appears in the editor. Remove the macro and observe what behavior you lose.

screens.title: Unreal Header Tool and Generated Code
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding how the Unreal Header Tool works clarifies why the macros are required. UHT scans C++ headers for UCLASS, UPROPERTY, and UFUNCTION markers and generates additional C++ files that register type information, property descriptors, and function dispatch code. The generated header is compiled with your project and supplies the runtime structures the engine uses to inspect classes. A concrete scenario: when you add UPROPERTY to a field, UHT emits code describing the property's name, type, and metadata flags. This enables editor details panels to enumerate properties and the serializer to read and write those values. A common misconception is to treat generated files as optional or purely cosmetic. They are not: without generated code the runtime cannot find or register those properties. Practically, this means you must include the generated header in your class file and follow the macro patterns UHT expects. If you see build errors referencing generated headers, it usually means UHT could not process the file due to syntax issues or missing macros. Closing thought: when you write headers, write them in the style UHT expects—clear macros, consistent placement of GENERATED_BODY or GENERATED_UCLASS_BODY—so the tool can produce correct runtime metadata. What build error would you expect if UHT failed to generate code for a new UCLASS?

keyIdea.title: UHT role
keyIdea.text: UHT produces generated headers registering classes and properties; these files enable runtime reflection, serialization, and editor features.

content.html:
Process Flow
Unreal Header Tool (UHT)
From annotated headers to compiled runtime metadata.
1
UHT parses headers for UCLASS/UPROPERTY/UFUNCTION.
2
It emits .generated.h files describing type and property metadata.
3
Generated code compiles into runtime registration structures that enable reflection and GC.
Concrete Example
Adding UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere) produces generated code with property metadata. That code lets the editor show the property and the serializer read/write it.
Misconception check
Generated headers are not optional plumbing; they are part of the compiled program that provides the reflection API the engine calls at runtime.
Build hint
If UHT fails, inspect your header for malformed macros or missing GENERATED_BODY. Fix syntax first, then rebuild to let UHT re-generate the glue code.
Key Takeaway

Write headers with the expected macros so UHT can generate the runtime metadata necessary for reflection and GC.

screens.title: Garbage Collection for UObjects
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal's garbage collector is a traversal-based system that operates over UObject instances. The GC marks live objects by starting from root objects—examples include UGameInstance, UWorld, and anything you explicitly add to the root set. From each root the collector traverses any references that the runtime knows about, such as UPROPERTY-marked pointers or entries in tracked containers. Any UObject reachable from a root remains alive. Conversely, if a UObject has no path from any root, it becomes eligible for collection on the next pass. A concrete example: if an actor owns a UObject via a UPROPERTY pointer, the actor is reachable in the world and therefore its owned UObject is reachable too. However, if you store a UObject* in a plain C++ pointer that is not a UPROPERTY, the GC will not see the reference; that object can be collected even though your pointer still points to its memory, which results in a dangling pointer and crashes. A common misconception is that GC behaves like a managed runtime that tracks every pointer; instead, the GC only considers references that are visible through the reflection metadata and known containers. Key takeaway: you must expose references to the collector with UPROPERTY or equivalent tracking to guarantee lifetime. Think about any raw UObject* in your codebase and ask: is it tracked? If not, convert it to a UPROPERTY or a weak pointer pattern when appropriate.

keyIdea.title: GC principle
keyIdea.text: GC keeps UObjects alive when they are reachable from root objects via tracked references; untracked pointers are invisible and lead to premature collection.

content.html:
Definition
Garbage Collection for UObjects
Reachability from roots determines whether a UObject is kept or reclaimed.
Root objects like UGameInstance or UWorld are always considered live. The GC performs a traversal from those roots using references exposed via UPROPERTY and tracked containers. Unreachable UObjects are candidates for collection.
Example: an actor with a UPROPERTY pointer to a UMyDataContainer keeps that container alive while the actor is reachable in the world.
Misconception: The GC does not see raw C++ pointers unless they are wrapped in tracked structures or marked with UPROPERTY. Missing these markers leads to dangling pointers.
Illustration
A short scenario: Actor A owns DataObject via UPROPERTY. Actor A is referenced by UWorld roots. DataObject is reachable and safe from GC. If DataObject is referenced only by an unmarked pointer, it is invisible to GC and can be collected while the pointer remains, causing a crash.
Practical check
Always mark UObject member pointers with UPROPERTY unless they are intentionally transient, and use TWeakObjectPtr for weak references that should not prevent collection.
Key Takeaway

GC relies on tracked references; missing UPROPERTY markers make references invisible and lead to premature collection.

Check Your Understanding

If a UObject keeps disappearing unexpectedly, what two things should you inspect first in your code?

screens.title: Root Objects and Reachability
screens.narratorSegment: Let's unpack the root set and why it matters. Roots are objects the GC treats as always live; typical examples include UWorld and UGameInstance. Code can also explicitly add objects to the root set via AddToRoot when you need an object to survive outside normal ownership hierarchies. From each root the GC traverses tracked references — UPROPERTY-marked pointers, TArrays that are themselves tracked via UPROPERTY, and other engine-managed containers — to mark reachable nodes. A concrete practice: if you create a UObject with NewObject and pass an Outer that is part of the world, the new object is reachable through the Outer and will not be collected while that Outer is alive. A common pitfall is adding objects to root without removing them, causing objects to never be collected and producing memory leaks. Use AddToRoot sparingly and only when an object genuinely needs lifetime beyond normal ownership. Another misconception is assuming only engine singletons are roots; while UWorld and UGameInstance are typical roots, you can create roots programmatically. Key takeaway: manage roots carefully: prefer proper Outer ownership and UPROPERTY tracking, and reserve AddToRoot for truly global objects. Consider: when would you prefer Outer ownership instead of adding to the root set?

keyIdea.title: Roots & reachability
keyIdea.text: Roots start GC traversal. Use Outer and UPROPERTY-based ownership to keep objects reachable; AddToRoot is for special cases and must be paired with careful removal.

content.html:
Process Flow
Root Objects and Reachability
How the GC finds live objects by traversing from roots through tracked references.
Roots: engine singletons like UWorld and UGameInstance, plus any object you AddToRoot. GC traversal begins at these roots.
Reachability: any object reachable via UPROPERTY or other tracked references remains alive. Choose Outer ownership to connect objects into reachable graphs.
Example: NewObject<UMyDataContainer>(this) creates an object whose Outer is the actor; while the actor is reachable the container stays alive.
Caution
AddToRoot prevents GC from collecting the object until you explicitly remove it. Overuse causes permanent growth of memory usage.
Practical tip
Prefer passing a sensible Outer and marking references with UPROPERTY instead of using global roots unless absolutely necessary.
Key Takeaway

Roots are the GC's starting points. Use Outer and UPROPERTY to attach objects to reachable graphs; use AddToRoot only for special global lifetimes.

screens.title: UPROPERTY: Why it matters for GC
screens.narratorSegment: This screen walks through a code example that demonstrates why UPROPERTY is essential for UObject member pointers. Imagine a class AMyActor that holds a UMyDataContainer* member. If you declare that member without UPROPERTY, the garbage collector cannot see the pointer as a tracked reference. That means the container could be collected while your pointer still holds its address. When you add UPROPERTY, UHT generates metadata so the GC visits that field during traversal and keeps the referenced object alive. A concrete code example is provided visually: declare UPROPERTY() UMyDataContainer* MyDataInstance; in the actor header and initialize it in BeginPlay with NewObject. After creating the instance, set a value and call PrintMyData; the engine will show the debug output verifying the object exists. A common misconception is that adding UPROPERTY is only for editor visibility. In practice, UPROPERTY also enables serialization and GC visibility. Also, marking everything with UPROPERTY indiscriminately can increase memory and metadata cost; annotate fields deliberately based on whether they must be tracked or serialized. Closing question: when you inspect a crash caused by an invalid UObject pointer, do you first check whether that pointer was declared with UPROPERTY or not? That check will often reveal the root cause.

narration.text: This screen walks through a code example that demonstrates why UPROPERTY is essential for UObject member pointers. Imagine a class AMyActor that holds a UMyDataContainer* member. If you declare that member without UPROPERTY, the garbage collector cannot see the pointer as a tracked reference. That means the container could be collected while your pointer still holds its address. When you add UPROPERTY, UHT generates metadata so the GC visits that field during traversal and keeps the referenced object alive. A concrete code example is provided visually: declare UPROPERTY() UMyDataContainer* MyDataInstance; in the actor header and initialize it in BeginPlay with NewObject. After creating the instance, set a value and call PrintMyData; the engine will show the debug output verifying the object exists. A common misconception is that adding UPROPERTY is only for editor visibility. In practice, UPROPERTY also enables serialization and GC visibility. Also, marking everything with UPROPERTY indiscriminately can increase memory and metadata cost; annotate fields deliberately based on whether they must be tracked or serialized. Closing question: when you inspect a crash caused by an invalid UObject pointer, do you first check whether that pointer was declared with UPROPERTY or not? That check will often reveal the root cause.

keyIdea.title: UPROPERTY for GC
keyIdea.text: UPROPERTY exposes member pointers to the reflection system so the garbage collector can traverse and retain referenced UObjects.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
UPROPERTY: Why it matters for GC
A minimal header and BeginPlay example showing correct declaration and instantiation.
Header (excerpt)
// MyInteractiveActor.h
UPROPERTY() // CORRECT: GC tracks this reference
UMyDataContainer* MyDataInstance;

UMyDataContainer* AnotherMeshComponent; // DANGEROUS: GC will NOT track this reference
BeginPlay (excerpt)
// MyInteractiveActor.cpp
void AMyInteractiveActor::BeginPlay()
{
  Super::BeginPlay();

  // Create an instance of UMyDataContainer
  MyDataInstance = NewObject<UMyDataContainer>(this); // 'this' is the Outer
  if (MyDataInstance)
  {
    MyDataInstance->MyIntValue = 42;
    MyDataInstance->PrintMyData();
  }
}
Misconception
UPROPERTY is not optional for GC tracking. If the field is important for object lifetime or serialization, annotate it.
Pro Tip

Use UPROPERTY for any UObject pointers that represent ownership or must survive GC; use TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning references.

Key Takeaway

UPROPERTY makes the difference between a safe reference and a dangling pointer when the GC runs.

screens.title: Creating UObjects with NewObject<T>()
screens.narratorSegment: Creating UObjects correctly is central to safe memory management. Unlike standard C++ objects, you should almost never use new to allocate a UObject. Instead, call NewObject (Outer) which performs required engine registration, initialization, and assigns an Outer that ties the object into the object hierarchy. A concrete example used earlier is NewObject<UMyDataContainer>(this) inside an actor; passing this as the Outer ensures the new object remains reachable while the actor is alive. If you use new, the engine does not register the instance and the GC will either ignore it or later crash because essential hooks were not called. A common misconception is to reserve NewObject for heavyweight assets; actually it is the standard pattern for any UObject instance you want the engine to manage. NewObject handles construction, links the instance into the outer chain, and ensures reflection metadata is available for serialization and GC. If you need a truly transient object not known to the engine, use a raw C++ type instead, or manage memory with C++ smart pointers for non-UObject classes. Closing question: when debugging lifetime bugs, do you confirm whether objects were created with NewObject or raw new? That check often reveals incorrect allocation patterns quickly.

keyIdea.title: NewObject usage
keyIdea.text: Use NewObject<T>(Outer) to create UObjects so they are registered, initialized, and attached in the object's Outer hierarchy for correct GC behavior.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Creating UObjects with NewObject
Correct instantiation pattern and the role of Outer.
// Correct: NewObject assigns Outer and registers with engine
UMyCustomObject* NewObjectInstance = NewObject<UMyCustomObject>(this);

// Incorrect: bypasses engine registration
UMyCustomObject* Leak = new UMyCustomObject();
Example explanation
NewObject registers the instance with the object system and sets a valid Outer. Using new bypasses those steps and produces objects not integrated with GC or reflection.
Ownership and Outer
Outer is the owning UObject. Choosing the correct Outer determines reachability: if the Outer is an actor or component that the world references, the created object stays alive while its Outer is reachable.
Misconception check
NewObject is not only for assets. Use it for any UObject you want the engine to manage and track via GC.
Key Takeaway

Prefer NewObject with a sensible Outer to ensure objects are registered and reachable; avoid new for UObjects.

screens.title: Common Memory Management Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: This slide compares the most common pitfalls you will encounter in Unreal C++ memory management. First, dangling pointers: if you hold a raw UObject* without UPROPERTY, the GC will not count it as a reference and the object may be collected, leaving your pointer pointing at freed memory. Example: a private member declared without UPROPERTY that you assume keeps an object alive. Second, using new: allocating a UObject with new bypasses engine initialization and registration, breaking reflection and GC. Example: new UMyObject() will not appear in serialized data and can cause crashes. Third, circular references: while UPROPERTY helps GC, complex circular ownership graphs sometimes make it difficult to determine when objects should be collected. For non-owning links in such graphs, use TWeakObjectPtr to avoid preventing collection. A misconception is to treat smart pointers from standard C++ as substitutes for UPROPERTY or engine-managed pointers. TSharedPtr and TUniquePtr are intended for non-UObject data and do not register references with the UObject GC. Key takeaways: always mark UObject members you want tracked with UPROPERTY, create UObjects with NewObject, and use weak pointers for non-owning relationships to avoid uncollectable cycles. When debugging, start by checking whether the pointer declarations and allocations conform to these rules.

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls summary
keyIdea.text: Dangling raw pointers, using new for UObjects, and circular references are the main sources of bugs; prefer UPROPERTY, NewObject, and TWeakObjectPtr when appropriate.

content.html:
Dangling Pointers
Raw UObject* members without UPROPERTY are invisible to GC and can point to freed memory when collection occurs.
Using new vs NewObject
new bypasses registration. NewObject registers with the engine and assigns an Outer for proper lifecycle management.
Circular References
Mutual UPROPERTY ownership can obscure when objects are unreachable. Use TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning links.
Concrete Example
If ComponentA holds a raw UMyObject* and ComponentB destroys the object, ComponentA's pointer becomes invalid. With UPROPERTY the GC would update the state and prevent premature collection while referenced.
Fixes
  • Mark member pointers with UPROPERTY.
  • Create UObjects with NewObject and pass a proper Outer.
  • Use TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning references to avoid cycles.

screens.title: Pointer Types: UObject vs C++ objects
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the correct pointer type is essential. For UObject-derived types that need engine features and GC tracking, use raw pointers as UPROPERTY() UMyType* or TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning references. UPROPERTY raw pointers are tracked by the GC when declared in UObjects. TWeakObjectPtr is a smart wrapper that safely becomes null when the referred UObject is collected, preventing dangling access. In contrast, TSharedPtr and TUniquePtr manage non-UObject C++ objects and rely on reference counting or unique ownership; they do not register with the UObject garbage collector. A concrete decision example: store runtime-configured data that requires no reflection and cannot be a UObject in a TUniquePtr. For UObject assets or engine-managed objects, use UPROPERTY or TWeakObjectPtr as appropriate. A common misconception is to use TSharedPtr for UObjects to get automatic lifetime; this won't register the pointer with the engine's GC and can produce inconsistent behavior. Key takeaway: match pointer semantics to object type—UPROPERTY and TWeakObjectPtr for UObjects, TSharedPtr/TUniquePtr for pure C++ objects. When in doubt, prefer UPROPERTY for members that represent ownership or persistence within the engine graph. Ask yourself: does this object need reflection, serialization, or GC? If yes, manage it as a UObject with engine-aware patterns.

keyIdea.title: Pointer guide
keyIdea.text: UPROPERTY and TWeakObjectPtr are for UObjects; TSharedPtr and TUniquePtr are for non-UObject C++ types. Use the right tool for the type to avoid lifetime bugs.

content.html:
UPROPERTY <UObject*>
Tracked by GC and serialized. Use for owned UObject members that need editor or runtime visibility.
TWeakObjectPtr<T>
Non-owning, becomes null when the UObject is collected, avoiding dangling pointers.
TSharedPtr / TUniquePtr
For pure C++ objects. Do not use these for UObjects since they do not register with the UObject GC.
Concrete Example
A cached UObject reference that should not keep the object alive can use TWeakObjectPtr. Persistent owned components should be UPROPERTY pointers so GC and serializer keep them safe.
Decision rule
If the object must be visible to the engine, use UObject patterns. If purely C++ with no engine integration, use standard smart pointers.

screens.title: Create and Use a UObject-derived Class
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough consolidates earlier theory into a specific workflow you can follow in the editor. Step one: create a new C++ class derived from UObject named UMyDataContainer. Step two: in the header add UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) int32 MyIntValue; and declare a UFUNCTION BlueprintCallable called PrintMyData. Step three: implement PrintMyData to log or show the value at runtime. Step four: in your actor's header add a member UPROPERTY() UMyDataContainer* MyDataInstance; and in BeginPlay call MyDataInstance = NewObject<UMyDataContainer>(this); set the integer and call PrintMyData. A concrete verification is to place the actor in a level and Play: you should see the debug message printed and a log entry confirming the UObject was created and invoked. A common mistake during this activity is forgetting GENERATED_BODY or misplacing includes so UHT cannot process the header; that produces compile or reflection errors. Also avoid creating the UObject via raw new. Key takeaway: this exercise demonstrates the full lifecycle—declare, annotate, generate, instantiate, and verify—so you can internalize safe patterns. After completing the workflow, ask: what would happen if MyDataInstance lacked UPROPERTY? That contrast helps cement the importance of the macro.

keyIdea.text: Follow create, annotate, NewObject, and verify steps to ensure your UObject is editor-visible and GC-safe.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Create and Use UMyDataContainer
Follow these steps inside the editor and codebase to validate UObject behavior.
1. Create a new C++ class derived from UObject called UMyDataContainer and add GENERATED_BODY.
2. Add UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) int32 MyIntValue; and UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable) void PrintMyData();
3. Implement PrintMyData to log the value with GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage and UE_LOG.
4. In your actor, add UPROPERTY() UMyDataContainer* MyDataInstance; then in BeginPlay call NewObject with this as the Outer, set the value, and invoke PrintMyData.
Code snippets
// UMyDataContainer.h excerpt
UCLASS(Blueprintable, BlueprintType)
class MYPROJECT_API UMyDataContainer : public UObject
{
  GENERATED_BODY()

public:
  UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Data")
  int32 MyIntValue;

  UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Data")
  void PrintMyData();
};
Verification

Place the actor in level, Play, and confirm the on-screen debug message and log line appear, proving the UObject was created and invoked correctly.

screens.title: Diagnosis and Fixes for Lifetime Bugs
screens.narratorSegment: When you encounter crashes or missing objects at runtime, follow a deliberate diagnosis path. First, check how the object was created: was it NewObject or raw new? If new was used for a UObject, the object is not registered and is likely the cause. Second, inspect the pointer declarations holding the object. If a UObject* member lacks UPROPERTY, the GC will not see it; adding UPROPERTY often resolves premature collection. Third, examine ownership and Outer: ensure the object has a valid Outer tied to a reachable object. Fourth, search for AddToRoot misuse: objects added to root must be removed when no longer needed or they will leak memory indefinitely. A concrete debugging example: a debug log reveals a null or invalid pointer after a GC pass; trace where the instance was created and whether UPROPERTY was used. A common misconception during debugging is to assume a memory leak is always caused by developers forgetting to free memory manually; with UObjects many issues stem from missing metadata or incorrect creation patterns rather than manual leaks. Closing practice: when you fix the code, re-run play and confirm the object remains available and no log errors appear. Which step will you check first next time you see an invalid UObject pointer?

keyIdea.text: Verify creation method, check UPROPERTY presence, confirm Outer and ownership, and avoid unnecessary AddToRoot to diagnose lifetime issues.

content.html:
Best Practice
Diagnosis and Fixes for Lifetime Bugs
A troubleshooting checklist to find and fix UObject lifetime issues.
1. Confirm creation: NewObject vs new. NewObject is required for engine-managed UObjects.
2. Check UPROPERTY: member pointers without UPROPERTY are invisible to GC.
3. Validate Outer: ensure the Outer is reachable so the object remains live.
4. Inspect AddToRoot usage: avoid permanent roots that cause leaks.
Concrete Example
If a UObject disappears after a GC pass, trace creation and declarations. If the pointer lacks UPROPERTY, add it and re-test. If AddToRoot was used, ensure a matching RemoveFromRoot when appropriate.
Misconception check
Not all crashes are due to missing delete calls. Many are caused by missing reflection metadata or incorrect allocation patterns that leave the GC blind to live references.
Key Takeaway

Use the checklist: creation method, UPROPERTY presence, Outer ownership, and root usage to diagnose and fix lifetime problems.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts. Third, Unreal's garbage collector tracks UObject lifetime by traversing from roots via tracked references; UPROPERTY is the main way to expose member pointers to the GC. A concrete reminder: always create UObjects with NewObject and provide a sensible Outer so objects are registered and reachable. Common pitfalls include creating UObjects with new, holding raw unmarked pointers that the GC cannot see, and misusing root objects which can leak memory. These concepts directly affect stability and editor workflows: using the correct macros and creation patterns prevents subtle runtime crashes and ensures your objects are editable, serializable, and safe from premature collection. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn why Unreal Engine uses a special object model built on top of C++ and how that model changes the way you create and hold references to objects. We start with the core claim: most engine-managed types must derive from the UObject base class. That one decision enables reflection, serialization, networking, editor integration, and a custom garbage collector that walks object references to reclaim memory safely. A concrete example you will practice later is creating a UMyDataContainer class derived from UObject, exposing an integer with UPROPERTY, and instantiating it with NewObject inside an actor. This pattern shows the full chain: UCLASS and UPROPERTY inform the reflection system, the Unreal Header Tool generates glue code, and NewObject registers the instance so the GC can track it. Why this matters in practice: if you use plain C++ new or keep a raw UObject* without UPROPERTY, the engine's GC cannot see the reference and the object can be collected unexpectedly, leading to crashes. A common misconception is to treat UObject pointers like regular pointers; they require the engine's metadata so lifetime is managed correctly. As you explore the screens ahead, watch for the rules around UPROPERTY, Outer objects, NewObject calls, and root objects. By the end you'll understand the safe creation pattern and how to avoid dangling pointers. Consider: what part of your current code would change if its objects needed reflection and GC tracking?

These objectives frame the skills you're about to practice. First, you'll explain the role of the UObject base class: not just a parent type but the foundation for reflection, GC, and editor integration. Understanding this clarifies why many engine systems expect UObject-derived types. Second, you will describe the reflection system and the meaning of UCLASS, UPROPERTY, and UFUNCTION. These macros produce metadata that the Unreal Header Tool parses and transforms into generated code, allowing runtime inspection, Blueprint exposure, and GC tracking. Third, you will understand Unreal's garbage collection for UObjects: how roots, reachability, and the GC pass determine which objects live or are reclaimed. You'll learn the rules that make objects collectible or safe. Fourth, you will identify common pitfalls like creating UObjects with new, missing UPROPERTY on member pointers, or mixing raw C++ smart pointers with engine GC. Each objective includes a concrete practice: create a UObject-derived class, add a UPROPERTY field, instantiate it with NewObject, and observe GC-safe behavior. A common misconception is assuming standard C++ memory rules apply unchanged; we'll contrast them with engine-managed lifetimes so you can avoid crashes and leaks. These objectives guide the hands-on steps later in the chapter.

Beyond explanation, this second set of objectives targets practical application. You will correctly use UPROPERTY on UObject member pointers so the garbage collector sees them. That practice includes declaring UPROPERTY for components or nested objects that your class owns. Next, you will instantiate UObjects with NewObject and pass a proper Outer so the created object joins the engine's object hierarchy. A concrete example: inside an actor's BeginPlay you will call NewObject<UMyDataContainer>(this), assign properties, and call a print function to verify the instance behaves as a managed UObject. You will also learn to detect and fix common pitfalls such as using new for UObjects or keeping non-UPROPERTY raw pointers to UObjects. A frequent misconception is to rely on standard smart pointers for UObjects; TSharedPtr and std::unique_ptr are for raw C++ types and do not register pointers with the UObject GC. Finally, you'll work with TWeakObjectPtr when you need non-owning references that must not prevent GC. Each skill is paired with a simple test: create, expose, instantiate, and validate behavior in the editor and during Play. This approach builds confidence and prevents lifetime-related bugs in your projects.

Start by grounding the definition: UObject is the engine's base class for objects that must be visible to the runtime systems. When a class derives from UObject it gains reflection metadata, serialization hooks, network replication support, editor integration, and eligibility for Unreal's garbage collection. Think of UObject as a contract with the engine: it promises the engine can inspect and manage instances. A concrete example is UActorComponent or UDataAsset; both derive from UObject and therefore appear in the editor and can be saved, replicated, and collected. One common misconception is that UObject is merely a naming convention or a thin wrapper over C++ objects. In reality, UObject participates in engine life-cycle events and requires special creation and ownership patterns. To make this practical, imagine you need a lightweight data holder that the editor can edit and Blueprints can call. You derive from UObject, annotate members with UPROPERTY to expose fields, and annotate functions with UFUNCTION for Blueprint calls. Then you create instances using NewObject so the engine registers them. Without deriving from UObject you lose those runtime features. Key takeaway: whenever a type must be inspected by the engine or be tracked by the GC, it should derive from UObject. Reflect on your recent classes: which need reflection or GC tracking and should therefore be refactored to inherit from UObject?

Now let's examine the reflection system and the role of the macros. The reflection system is how Unreal learns about your classes, properties, and functions at runtime. When you add UCLASS, UPROPERTY, or UFUNCTION to your header, the Unreal Header Tool parses those markers and generates additional C++ code — the generated header files — which register type information and property metadata with the engine. A concrete example: declaring UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere) float MyValue declares the property and attaches editor metadata so it appears in Details panels. Importantly, UPROPERTY also signals to the garbage collector that a pointer member should be treated as a live reference. A common misconception is that UPROPERTY only affects editor exposure; in truth it also influences GC behavior and serialization. Practically, this means you should annotate any UObject* members you expect the GC to consider. UFUNCTION controls whether functions are callable from Blueprints or network-replicable depending on flags. The reflection glue enables dynamic creation by name, property iteration, and serialization. If you remove the macros, the engine cannot generate the required metadata and those runtime features break. As you code, treat the macros as both administrative and functional: they change how the engine treats your types, not just how the editor displays them. Reflect on a recent property: would the engine need to see it? If yes, annotate it with UPROPERTY and choose the correct metadata flags.

Understanding how the Unreal Header Tool works clarifies why the macros are required. UHT scans C++ headers for UCLASS, UPROPERTY, and UFUNCTION markers and generates additional C++ files that register type information, property descriptors, and function dispatch code. The generated header is compiled with your project and supplies the runtime structures the engine uses to inspect classes. A concrete scenario: when you add UPROPERTY to a field, UHT emits code describing the property's name, type, and metadata flags. This enables editor details panels to enumerate properties and the serializer to read and write those values. A common misconception is to treat generated files as optional or purely cosmetic. They are not: without generated code the runtime cannot find or register those properties. Practically, this means you must include the generated header in your class file and follow the macro patterns UHT expects. If you see build errors referencing generated headers, it usually means UHT could not process the file due to syntax issues or missing macros. Closing thought: when you write headers, write them in the style UHT expects—clear macros, consistent placement of GENERATED_BODY or GENERATED_UCLASS_BODY—so the tool can produce correct runtime metadata. What build error would you expect if UHT failed to generate code for a new UCLASS?

Unreal's garbage collector is a traversal-based system that operates over UObject instances. The GC marks live objects by starting from root objects—examples include UGameInstance, UWorld, and anything you explicitly add to the root set. From each root the collector traverses any references that the runtime knows about, such as UPROPERTY-marked pointers or entries in tracked containers. Any UObject reachable from a root remains alive. Conversely, if a UObject has no path from any root, it becomes eligible for collection on the next pass. A concrete example: if an actor owns a UObject via a UPROPERTY pointer, the actor is reachable in the world and therefore its owned UObject is reachable too. However, if you store a UObject* in a plain C++ pointer that is not a UPROPERTY, the GC will not see the reference; that object can be collected even though your pointer still points to its memory, which results in a dangling pointer and crashes. A common misconception is that GC behaves like a managed runtime that tracks every pointer; instead, the GC only considers references that are visible through the reflection metadata and known containers. Key takeaway: you must expose references to the collector with UPROPERTY or equivalent tracking to guarantee lifetime. Think about any raw UObject* in your codebase and ask: is it tracked? If not, convert it to a UPROPERTY or a weak pointer pattern when appropriate.

Let's unpack the root set and why it matters. Roots are objects the GC treats as always live; typical examples include UWorld and UGameInstance. Code can also explicitly add objects to the root set via AddToRoot when you need an object to survive outside normal ownership hierarchies. From each root the GC traverses tracked references — UPROPERTY-marked pointers, TArrays that are themselves tracked via UPROPERTY, and other engine-managed containers — to mark reachable nodes. A concrete practice: if you create a UObject with NewObject and pass an Outer that is part of the world, the new object is reachable through the Outer and will not be collected while that Outer is alive. A common pitfall is adding objects to root without removing them, causing objects to never be collected and producing memory leaks. Use AddToRoot sparingly and only when an object genuinely needs lifetime beyond normal ownership. Another misconception is assuming only engine singletons are roots; while UWorld and UGameInstance are typical roots, you can create roots programmatically. Key takeaway: manage roots carefully: prefer proper Outer ownership and UPROPERTY tracking, and reserve AddToRoot for truly global objects. Consider: when would you prefer Outer ownership instead of adding to the root set?

This screen walks through a code example that demonstrates why UPROPERTY is essential for UObject member pointers. Imagine a class AMyActor that holds a UMyDataContainer* member. If you declare that member without UPROPERTY, the garbage collector cannot see the pointer as a tracked reference. That means the container could be collected while your pointer still holds its address. When you add UPROPERTY, UHT generates metadata so the GC visits that field during traversal and keeps the referenced object alive. A concrete code example is provided visually: declare UPROPERTY() UMyDataContainer* MyDataInstance; in the actor header and initialize it in BeginPlay with NewObject. After creating the instance, set a value and call PrintMyData; the engine will show the debug output verifying the object exists. A common misconception is that adding UPROPERTY is only for editor visibility. In practice, UPROPERTY also enables serialization and GC visibility. Also, marking everything with UPROPERTY indiscriminately can increase memory and metadata cost; annotate fields deliberately based on whether they must be tracked or serialized. Closing question: when you inspect a crash caused by an invalid UObject pointer, do you first check whether that pointer was declared with UPROPERTY or not? That check will often reveal the root cause.

Creating UObjects correctly is central to safe memory management. Unlike standard C++ objects, you should almost never use new to allocate a UObject. Instead, call NewObject (Outer) which performs required engine registration, initialization, and assigns an Outer that ties the object into the object hierarchy. A concrete example used earlier is NewObject<UMyDataContainer>(this) inside an actor; passing this as the Outer ensures the new object remains reachable while the actor is alive. If you use new, the engine does not register the instance and the GC will either ignore it or later crash because essential hooks were not called. A common misconception is to reserve NewObject for heavyweight assets; actually it is the standard pattern for any UObject instance you want the engine to manage. NewObject handles construction, links the instance into the outer chain, and ensures reflection metadata is available for serialization and GC. If you need a truly transient object not known to the engine, use a raw C++ type instead, or manage memory with C++ smart pointers for non-UObject classes. Closing question: when debugging lifetime bugs, do you confirm whether objects were created with NewObject or raw new? That check often reveals incorrect allocation patterns quickly.

This slide compares the most common pitfalls you will encounter in Unreal C++ memory management. First, dangling pointers: if you hold a raw UObject* without UPROPERTY, the GC will not count it as a reference and the object may be collected, leaving your pointer pointing at freed memory. Example: a private member declared without UPROPERTY that you assume keeps an object alive. Second, using new: allocating a UObject with new bypasses engine initialization and registration, breaking reflection and GC. Example: new UMyObject() will not appear in serialized data and can cause crashes. Third, circular references: while UPROPERTY helps GC, complex circular ownership graphs sometimes make it difficult to determine when objects should be collected. For non-owning links in such graphs, use TWeakObjectPtr to avoid preventing collection. A misconception is to treat smart pointers from standard C++ as substitutes for UPROPERTY or engine-managed pointers. TSharedPtr and TUniquePtr are intended for non-UObject data and do not register references with the UObject GC. Key takeaways: always mark UObject members you want tracked with UPROPERTY, create UObjects with NewObject, and use weak pointers for non-owning relationships to avoid uncollectable cycles. When debugging, start by checking whether the pointer declarations and allocations conform to these rules.

Choosing the correct pointer type is essential. For UObject-derived types that need engine features and GC tracking, use raw pointers as UPROPERTY() UMyType* or TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning references. UPROPERTY raw pointers are tracked by the GC when declared in UObjects. TWeakObjectPtr is a smart wrapper that safely becomes null when the referred UObject is collected, preventing dangling access. In contrast, TSharedPtr and TUniquePtr manage non-UObject C++ objects and rely on reference counting or unique ownership; they do not register with the UObject garbage collector. A concrete decision example: store runtime-configured data that requires no reflection and cannot be a UObject in a TUniquePtr. For UObject assets or engine-managed objects, use UPROPERTY or TWeakObjectPtr as appropriate. A common misconception is to use TSharedPtr for UObjects to get automatic lifetime; this won't register the pointer with the engine's GC and can produce inconsistent behavior. Key takeaway: match pointer semantics to object type—UPROPERTY and TWeakObjectPtr for UObjects, TSharedPtr/TUniquePtr for pure C++ objects. When in doubt, prefer UPROPERTY for members that represent ownership or persistence within the engine graph. Ask yourself: does this object need reflection, serialization, or GC? If yes, manage it as a UObject with engine-aware patterns.

This hands-on walkthrough consolidates earlier theory into a specific workflow you can follow in the editor. Step one: create a new C++ class derived from UObject named UMyDataContainer. Step two: in the header add UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite) int32 MyIntValue; and declare a UFUNCTION BlueprintCallable called PrintMyData. Step three: implement PrintMyData to log or show the value at runtime. Step four: in your actor's header add a member UPROPERTY() UMyDataContainer* MyDataInstance; and in BeginPlay call MyDataInstance = NewObject<UMyDataContainer>(this); set the integer and call PrintMyData. A concrete verification is to place the actor in a level and Play: you should see the debug message printed and a log entry confirming the UObject was created and invoked. A common mistake during this activity is forgetting GENERATED_BODY or misplacing includes so UHT cannot process the header; that produces compile or reflection errors. Also avoid creating the UObject via raw new. Key takeaway: this exercise demonstrates the full lifecycle—declare, annotate, generate, instantiate, and verify—so you can internalize safe patterns. After completing the workflow, ask: what would happen if MyDataInstance lacked UPROPERTY? That contrast helps cement the importance of the macro.

When you encounter crashes or missing objects at runtime, follow a deliberate diagnosis path. First, check how the object was created: was it NewObject or raw new? If new was used for a UObject, the object is not registered and is likely the cause. Second, inspect the pointer declarations holding the object. If a UObject* member lacks UPROPERTY, the GC will not see it; adding UPROPERTY often resolves premature collection. Third, examine ownership and Outer: ensure the object has a valid Outer tied to a reachable object. Fourth, search for AddToRoot misuse: objects added to root must be removed when no longer needed or they will leak memory indefinitely. A concrete debugging example: a debug log reveals a null or invalid pointer after a GC pass; trace where the instance was created and whether UPROPERTY was used. A common misconception during debugging is to assume a memory leak is always caused by developers forgetting to free memory manually; with UObjects many issues stem from missing metadata or incorrect creation patterns rather than manual leaks. Closing practice: when you fix the code, re-run play and confirm the object remains available and no log errors appear. Which step will you check first next time you see an invalid UObject pointer?

Let's summarize the essential concepts. First, UObject is the engine-managed base class that enables reflection, serialization, networking, editor integration, and garbage collection. Second, the reflection system uses UCLASS, UPROPERTY, and UFUNCTION macros; UHT parses these markers and generates glue code enabling runtime metadata and editor features. Third, Unreal's garbage collector tracks UObject lifetime by traversing from roots via tracked references; UPROPERTY is the main way to expose member pointers to the GC. A concrete reminder: always create UObjects with NewObject and provide a sensible Outer so objects are registered and reachable. Common pitfalls include creating UObjects with new, holding raw unmarked pointers that the GC cannot see, and misusing root objects which can leak memory. These concepts directly affect stability and editor workflows: using the correct macros and creation patterns prevents subtle runtime crashes and ensures your objects are editable, serializable, and safe from premature collection. Closing reflection: which pattern will you adopt immediately to make your code safer—UPROPERTY on members, NewObject for creation, or TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning references?

A final quick reference to carry forward. First, UPROPERTY is your primary tool to make member pointers visible to the engine and GC; use it for ownership and serialized fields. Second, always create UObjects with NewObject and supply a sensible Outer so instances are registered and reachable by the GC. Third, choose pointer types intentionally: use TWeakObjectPtr for non-owning UObject references and TSharedPtr or TUniquePtr for non-UObject C++ memory. These three rules cover the majority of lifetime and reflection issues developers face in Unreal C++ projects. Keep them in mind when designing systems: marking fields intentionally and following creation conventions prevents crashes and makes your code editor-friendly. Which of these will you check first when reviewing a teammate's code? This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
